sections.title: Diode Operation
sections.summary: A diode has two regions (anode/p-side, cathode/n-side) forming a single pn junction. Forward bias (positive at anode, negative at cathode) allows conduction; reverse bias blocks it. Two current types: electron and hole. Silicon barrier potential ≈ 0.7 V.

sections.title: V-I Characteristics
sections.summary: The V-I curve plots diode current vs. voltage. Forward region: little current until barrier potential is reached, then current rises steeply. Reverse region: tiny minority-carrier current until breakdown. Dynamic resistance r'd matters in forward bias above the knee.

sections.title: Diode Models
sections.summary: Ideal model: diode = switch (closed forward, open reverse). Practical model: adds 0.7 V barrier potential. Complete model: adds forward dynamic resistance r'd AND reverse resistance. Pick the model based on required precision.

sections.title: Half-Wave Rectifiers
sections.summary: Single diode conducts during one half of the input cycle. V_avg = V_p/π ≈ 0.318·V_p. Output frequency = input frequency. PIV = V_p(secondary). Practical V_p(out) = V_p(in) − 0.7 V.

sections.title: Full-Wave Rectifiers
sections.summary: Both halves of input produce output. Output frequency = 2·f_in. V_avg = 2V_p/π ≈ 0.637·V_p. Center-tap: 2 diodes, PIV = 2·V_p(out) + 0.7. Bridge: 4 diodes, PIV ≈ V_p(out), drop = 1.4 V (two diodes conduct each half-cycle).

sections.title: Power Supply Filters & Regulators
sections.summary: Capacitor-input filter smooths rectified output toward V_peak. Ripple voltage V_r ≈ V_p/(f·R_L·C) — larger C, larger R_L, or higher f all reduce ripple. Ripple factor r = V_r(pp)/V_DC. Line regulation: ΔV_out/ΔV_in. Load regulation: change in V_out vs. change in I_load.

sections.title: Limiters & Clampers
sections.summary: Limiter (clipper): cuts off part of a waveform above/below a level. Bias voltage shifts the clipping level. Clamper: ADDS a dc level to a waveform (uses a capacitor to store charge). Positive clamper makes negative peak ≈ +0.7 V; output dc value ≈ V_p − 0.7.

sections.title: Voltage Multipliers
sections.summary: Use diodes and capacitors to produce dc output greater than peak input. Doubler: 2·V_p. Tripler: 3·V_p. Quadrupler: 4·V_p. Common in high-voltage low-current applications like CRT displays.

sections.title: The Diode Datasheet
sections.summary: Key ratings: V_F (forward voltage drop), I_F(max) (max forward current), V_R(max) or PIV (max reverse voltage), I_R (reverse leakage). Always design with margin below max ratings.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.summary: DMM diode test: good forward = ~0.7 V; open junction = OL; shorted junction = 0 V. Open transformer secondary → 0 V output. Open diode in bridge → output becomes half-wave (60 Hz ripple instead of 120 Hz on a 60 Hz line). Cap leak → excess ripple.

questions.text: The two regions of a diode are the anode and the collector.
questions.explanation: The two regions are anode (p-side) and cathode (n-side). 'Collector' is a BJT terminal, not a diode terminal.

questions.text: A diode can conduct current in two directions with equal ease.
questions.explanation: A diode is fundamentally a one-way device — it conducts only when forward-biased and blocks current when reverse-biased.

questions.text: A diode conducts current when forward-biased.
questions.explanation: Forward bias (positive at anode, negative at cathode) reduces the depletion region and allows majority carriers to cross the junction.

questions.text: When reverse-biased, a diode ideally appears as a short.
questions.explanation: Ideally, a reverse-biased diode appears as an OPEN switch (infinite resistance, no current). A short would be the forward-bias ideal.

questions.text: Two types of current in a diode are electron and hole.
questions.explanation: Electron current flows in the n-region (electrons are majority carriers); hole current flows in the p-region (holes are majority carriers). Both contribute to total diode current.

questions.text: A basic half-wave rectifier consists of one diode.
questions.explanation: Half-wave = one diode + one load resistor. The diode conducts during one half of the input cycle and blocks the other.

questions.text: The output frequency of a half-wave rectifier is twice the input frequency.
questions.explanation: Half-wave output frequency EQUALS the input frequency — only one pulse per cycle. Doubling the frequency is a full-wave property.

questions.text: The diode in a half-wave rectifier conducts for half the input cycle.
questions.explanation: The diode forward-biases and conducts during one half-cycle (typically the positive), and reverse-biases and blocks during the other.

questions.text: PIV stands for positive inverse voltage.
questions.explanation: PIV stands for PEAK Inverse Voltage — the maximum reverse-bias voltage the diode must withstand without breaking down.

questions.text: Each diode in a full-wave rectifier conducts for the entire input cycle.
questions.explanation: Each diode conducts for HALF the input cycle. The two halves are combined to produce continuous output, but no single diode is on the whole time.

questions.text: The output frequency of a full-wave rectifier is twice the input frequency.
questions.explanation: Full-wave produces two output pulses per input cycle, so f_out = 2·f_in. A 60 Hz input gives 120 Hz output — easier to filter than 60 Hz.

questions.text: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes.
questions.explanation: Bridge rectifier = 4 diodes arranged in a bridge configuration; two conduct on each half-cycle (diagonal pairs).

questions.text: In a bridge rectifier, two diodes conduct during each half-cycle of the input.
questions.explanation: Diagonal pairs of diodes alternate conducting on each half-cycle, which is why bridge rectifiers drop 1.4 V (two 0.7 V drops in series) rather than 0.7 V.

questions.text: The purpose of the capacitor filter in a rectifier is to convert ac to dc.
questions.explanation: The RECTIFIER converts ac to pulsating dc. The capacitor filter SMOOTHS the pulsating dc into a more constant dc by storing charge and supplying it during the dips.

questions.text: The output voltage of a filtered rectifier always has some ripple voltage.
questions.explanation: Some ripple is unavoidable — the capacitor must discharge slightly between pulses to deliver load current. Larger C and R_L reduce ripple but never eliminate it.

questions.text: A smaller filter capacitor reduces the ripple.
questions.explanation: Reverse: V_r ≈ V_p/(f·R_L·C). Ripple is INVERSELY proportional to C, so a LARGER capacitor reduces ripple. Smaller capacitors give worse smoothing.

questions.text: Line and load regulation are the same.
questions.explanation: Line regulation tracks how V_out responds to changes in INPUT voltage. Load regulation tracks how V_out responds to changes in LOAD CURRENT. Different inputs, different specs.

questions.text: A diode limiter is also known as a clipper.
questions.explanation: Limiter and clipper are interchangeable names for circuits that cut off (clip) part of a waveform above or below a reference level.

questions.text: The purpose of a clamper is to remove a dc level from a waveform.
questions.explanation: A clamper ADDS a dc level to a waveform (shifting it up or down). Removing dc is what a coupling capacitor does — opposite function.

questions.text: Voltage multipliers use diodes and capacitors.
questions.explanation: Doublers, triplers, and quadruplers all combine diodes (for unidirectional charging) and capacitors (for storing charge in series), producing a dc output that is a multiple of the peak input.

questions.text: When a diode is forward-biased and the bias voltage is increased, the forward current will
questions.explanation: Once past the barrier potential, more bias voltage drives more current through the limiting resistor — they're directly related (Ohm's law on the rest of the circuit).

questions.text: When a diode is forward-biased and the bias voltage is increased, the voltage across the diode (assuming the practical model) will
questions.explanation: Practical model: V_F is fixed at 0.7 V regardless of current. The extra voltage drops across the series resistor, not the diode. (This was the trap on Practice Quiz #2 Q17.)

questions.text: When a diode is reverse-biased and the bias voltage is increased, the reverse current (assuming the practical model) will
questions.explanation: Practical model treats a reverse-biased diode as an open switch — I_R = 0 regardless of bias. (Until breakdown, which is outside the model's scope.)

questions.text: When a diode is reverse-biased and the bias voltage is increased, the reverse current (assuming the complete model) will
questions.explanation: Complete model includes finite reverse resistance, so I_R = V_R/R_reverse — small but nonzero, and increases with V_R.

questions.text: When a diode is forward-biased and the bias voltage is increased, the voltage across the diode (assuming the complete model) will
questions.explanation: Complete model: V_F = 0.7 V + I_F·r'_d. As more current flows, the drop across r'_d grows, so total V_F slightly increases. (Compare to Q2: practical model says no change.)

questions.text: If the forward current in a diode is increased, the diode voltage (assuming the practical model) will
questions.explanation: Practical model fixes V_F at 0.7 V regardless of current. Same idea as Q2 — that's the whole point of the simplification.

questions.text: If the forward current in a diode is decreased, the diode voltage (assuming the complete model) will
questions.explanation: Complete model: V_F = 0.7 + I_F·r'_d. Less current means a smaller drop across r'_d, so V_F decreases slightly toward 0.7 V.

questions.text: If the barrier potential of a diode is exceeded, the forward current will
questions.explanation: Below the barrier potential the diode is essentially off. Once exceeded, the diode 'turns on' and current rises steeply with voltage (the knee of the V-I curve).

questions.text: If the input voltage in Figure 2–28 is increased, the peak inverse voltage across the diode will
questions.explanation: PIV in a half-wave rectifier ≈ V_p(secondary). Higher input → higher secondary peak → higher PIV across the off diode.

questions.text: If the turns ratio of the transformer in Figure 2–28 is decreased, the forward current through the diode will
questions.explanation: Floyd defines n = N_sec/N_pri. A smaller n means a smaller secondary voltage, so smaller V_p drives less current through the diode and load.

questions.text: If the frequency of the input voltage in Figure 2–36 is increased, the output voltage will
questions.explanation: Average dc output of a full-wave rectifier depends on PEAK amplitude, not frequency. Frequency affects ripple in a filtered supply, but not the rectified output amplitude itself.

questions.text: If the PIV rating of the diodes in Figure 2–36 is increased, the current through R_L will
questions.explanation: PIV is a maximum-rating spec — a ceiling, not an operating value. Using diodes with higher PIV ratings gives more safety margin but doesn't change actual circuit current.

questions.text: If one of the diodes in Figure 2–41 opens, the average voltage to the load will
questions.explanation: Bridge with one open diode = half-wave operation (only one half-cycle gets through). Average drops from 0.637·V_p to 0.318·V_p — roughly halved.

questions.text: If the value of R_L in Figure 2–41 is decreased, the current through each diode will
questions.explanation: Smaller R_L means more load current. Each conducting diode pair carries that load current, so diode current increases.

questions.text: If the capacitor value in Figure 2–48 is decreased, the output ripple voltage will
questions.explanation: V_r ≈ V_p/(f·R_L·C). Smaller C means the cap discharges more between pulses, producing larger ripple.

questions.text: If the line voltage in Figure 2–51 is increased, ideally the +5 V output will
questions.explanation: That's the entire point of a regulator — it holds V_out constant despite changes in input voltage. Ideal line regulation = 0%.

questions.text: If the bias voltage in Figure 2–55 is decreased, the positive portion of the output voltage will
questions.explanation: Figure 2-55 is a biased positive limiter — the positive clip level = V_BIAS + 0.7 V. Lower bias means the positive side gets clipped at a lower level, so the positive output decreases.

questions.text: If the bias voltage in Figure 2–55 is increased, the negative portion of the output voltage will
questions.explanation: Bias only affects the positive-clipping side. The negative half-cycle passes through unaffected by bias changes.

questions.text: If the value of R3 in Figure 2–61 is decreased, the positive output voltage will
questions.explanation: Voltage-divider biased limiter: bias level = V_supply·R3/(R2+R3). Smaller R3 lowers the bias, which lowers the positive clip level, so the positive output decreases.

questions.text: If the input voltage in Figure 2–65 is increased, the peak negative value of the output voltage will
questions.explanation: Voltage-multiplier output peak scales directly with input peak. Larger input → larger negative peak magnitude (more negative).

questions.text: The term bias means
options: the ratio of majority carriers to minority carriers
the amount of current across a diode
a dc voltage that is applied to control the operation of a device
questions.explanation: Bias is a dc voltage applied to set the operating condition of a device — forward-bias to turn on, reverse-bias to turn off.

questions.text: To forward-bias a diode,
options: an external voltage is applied that is positive at the anode and negative at the cathode
an external voltage is applied that is negative at the anode and positive at the cathode
an external voltage is applied that is positive at the p region and negative at the n region
questions.explanation: Anode = p-region, cathode = n-region. (a) and (c) say the same thing two ways. Both true → answer is (d).

questions.text: When a diode is forward-biased,
options: the only current is hole current
the only current is electron current
the only current is produced by majority carriers
the current is produced by both holes and electrons
questions.explanation: Both carrier types contribute: electrons flow from n to p, holes flow from p to n. Total current is the sum of both.

questions.text: Although current is blocked in reverse bias,
options: there is some current due to majority carriers
there is a very small current due to minority carriers
questions.explanation: Thermally generated minority carriers produce a tiny reverse saturation current (typically nA range). Avalanche only occurs at breakdown voltages, not normal reverse bias.

questions.text: For a silicon diode, the value of the forward-bias voltage typically
options: depends on the width of the depletion region
depends on the concentration of majority carriers
questions.explanation: Silicon barrier potential ≈ 0.7 V. Below this, the depletion region blocks conduction; above it, the diode turns on. (0.3 V is germanium.)

questions.text: When forward-biased, a diode
questions.explanation: Forward bias overcomes the barrier potential, collapsing the depletion region and allowing majority carriers to flow — the diode conducts.

questions.text: A diode is normally operated in
questions.explanation: Normal operation is forward OR reverse bias. Reverse breakdown is reserved for special devices (zeners). A regular rectifier diode swings between forward and reverse during AC operation.

questions.text: The dynamic resistance can be important when a diode is
questions.explanation: r'_d is the slope of the V-I curve in the forward region above the knee. It matters when modeling small voltage changes for nonzero forward currents.

questions.text: The V-I curve for a diode shows
options: the voltage across the diode for a given current
the amount of current for a given bias voltage
questions.explanation: Per Floyd's text, the V-I curve is read as V across the diode for a given I. (Both (a) and (b) describe valid uses of the curve, but the textbook answer is (a).)

questions.text: Ideally, a diode can be represented by a
questions.explanation: Ideal diode model: a perfect switch — closed (zero drop, any current) when forward-biased, open (zero current, any voltage) when reverse-biased.

questions.text: In the practical diode model,
options: the barrier potential is taken into account
the forward dynamic resistance is taken into account
questions.explanation: Practical model adds ONLY the 0.7 V barrier potential to the ideal switch — it doesn't include r'_d. (That's the COMPLETE model.) This was the trap on Practice Quiz #2 Q29.

questions.text: In the complete diode model,
options: the barrier potential is taken into account
the forward dynamic resistance is taken into account
the reverse resistance is taken into account
questions.explanation: Complete model = barrier potential + forward dynamic resistance r'_d + finite reverse resistance R_R. The most accurate of the three models.

questions.text: The average value of a half-wave rectified voltage with a peak value of 200 V is
questions.explanation: V_avg(half-wave) = V_p/π = 200/π ≈ 63.66 V ≈ 63.7 V. The 0.318 multiplier comes from 1/π.

questions.text: When a 60 Hz sinusoidal voltage is applied to the input of a half-wave rectifier, the output frequency is
questions.explanation: Half-wave preserves input frequency — one input cycle produces one output pulse. (Full-wave would double it to 120 Hz.)

questions.text: The peak value of the input to a half-wave rectifier is 10 V. The approximate peak value of the output is
questions.explanation: Practical model: V_p(out) = V_p(in) − 0.7 = 10 − 0.7 = 9.3 V. The diode 'eats' 0.7 V to conduct.

questions.text: For the circuit in Question 15, the diode must be able to withstand a reverse voltage of
questions.explanation: Half-wave PIV ≈ V_p(input) = 10 V. When the diode is reverse-biased, the full input peak appears across it.

questions.text: The average value of a full-wave rectified voltage with a peak value of 75 V is
questions.explanation: V_avg(full-wave) = 2V_p/π = 2·75/π ≈ 47.75 V ≈ 47.8 V. Twice the half-wave average because both halves contribute.

questions.text: When a 60 Hz sinusoidal voltage is applied to the input of a full-wave rectifier, the output frequency is
questions.explanation: Full-wave produces two output pulses per input cycle, so f_out = 2·f_in = 120 Hz. Easier to filter than 60 Hz half-wave output.

questions.text: The total secondary voltage in a center-tapped full-wave rectifier is 125 V rms. Neglecting the diode drop, the rms output voltage is
questions.explanation: Center-tap splits the secondary in half — each half = 125/2 = 62.5 V rms. The output is full-wave rectified from one half at a time, so output rms = 62.5 V.

questions.text: When the peak output voltage is 100 V, the PIV for each diode in a center-tapped full-wave rectifier is (neglecting the diode drop)
questions.explanation: Center-tap PIV = 2·V_p(out) = 2·100 = 200 V. The off diode sees the full secondary plus the conducting diode's output — twice the peak.

questions.text: When the rms output voltage of a bridge full-wave rectifier is 20 V, the peak inverse voltage across the diodes is (neglecting the diode drop)
questions.explanation: Bridge PIV ≈ V_p(out) = V_rms·√2 = 20·1.414 ≈ 28.3 V. (Bridge PIV is half what a center-tap would need for the same output — major advantage.)

questions.text: The ideal dc output voltage of a capacitor-input filter is equal to
options: the peak value of the rectified voltage
the average value of the rectified voltage
the rms value of the rectified voltage
questions.explanation: Ideally, the cap charges to V_peak and stays there (no discharge between pulses). Real filters fall slightly below peak due to ripple, but ideal = V_peak.

questions.text: A certain power-supply filter produces an output with a ripple of 100 mV peak-to-peak and a dc value of 20 V. The ripple factor is
questions.explanation: r = V_r(pp)/V_DC = 0.1 V / 20 V = 0.005. Watch the unit conversion — 100 mV = 0.1 V, not 100 V. (This was a Practice Quiz #2 weak spot.)

questions.text: A 60 V peak full-wave rectified voltage is applied to a capacitor-input filter. If f = 120 Hz, R_L = 10 kΩ, and C = 10 μF, the ripple voltage is
If the load resistance of a capacitor-filtered full-wave rectifier is reduced, the ripple voltage
questions.explanation: V_r ∝ 1/R_L. Smaller R_L means more load current, which discharges the cap faster between pulses → larger ripple.

questions.text: Line regulation is determined by
options: changes in load resistance and output voltage
changes in output voltage and input voltage
questions.explanation: Line regulation = ΔV_out/ΔV_in × 100%. It measures how well V_out resists changes in input voltage. Load is irrelevant — that's load regulation.

questions.text: Load regulation is determined by
options: changes in load current and input voltage
changes in load current and output voltage
changes in load resistance and input voltage
changes in zener current and load current
questions.explanation: Load regulation = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100%, with input voltage held constant. It measures how V_out responds to load current changes.

questions.text: A 10 V peak-to-peak sinusoidal voltage is applied across a silicon diode and series resistor. The maximum voltage across the diode is
questions.explanation: 10 V peak-to-peak means ±5 V peaks. On the forward half the diode drops only 0.7 V; on the reverse half the diode is OFF and the full negative peak (5 V) drops across it. Max = 5 V.

questions.text: In a certain biased limiter, the bias voltage is 5 V and the input is a 10 V peak sine wave. If the positive terminal of the bias voltage is connected to the cathode of the diode, the maximum voltage at the anode is
questions.explanation: Cathode is held at +5 V. The diode conducts only when V_anode > V_cathode + 0.7 = 5.7 V, clamping anything above that. Max V_anode = 5.7 V.

questions.text: In a certain positive clamper circuit, a 120 V rms sine wave is applied to the input. The dc value of the output is
questions.explanation: Positive clamper shifts the wave so the negative peak sits at +0.7 V. DC value of output ≈ V_p − 0.7 = (120·√2) − 0.7 ≈ 169.7 − 0.7 ≈ 169 V.

questions.text: The input of a voltage doubler is 120 V rms. The dc output is approximately
questions.explanation: Doubler output ≈ 2·V_p = 2·(120·√2) = 2·169.7 ≈ 339 V. Don't confuse rms with peak — the doubler doubles the PEAK, not the rms.

questions.text: If the input voltage to a voltage tripler has an rms value of 12 V, the dc output voltage is approximately
questions.explanation: Tripler output ≈ 3·V_p = 3·(12·√2) = 3·16.97 ≈ 50.9 V. Same trap as Q31 — multiply the peak, not the rms.

questions.text: When a silicon diode is working properly in forward bias, a DMM in the diode test position will indicate
questions.explanation: DMM diode test injects a small forward current and reads the resulting voltage. A healthy silicon junction shows ~0.7 V; germanium would show ~0.3 V.

questions.text: When a silicon diode is open, a DMM will generally indicate
questions.explanation: Open junction = infinite resistance = no current path = OL (over-limit) on the DMM. A shorted junction would show 0 V instead.

questions.text: In a rectifier circuit, if the secondary winding in the transformer opens, the output is
questions.explanation: Open secondary = no AC reaches the rectifier = no rectified output. The whole signal path is broken at the source.

questions.text: If one of the diodes in a bridge full-wave rectifier opens, the output is
options: one-fourth the amplitude of the input voltage
questions.explanation: Bridge with one open diode degrades to half-wave operation — only one diagonal pair functions, so only one half-cycle gets through.

questions.text: If you are checking a 60 Hz full-wave bridge rectifier and observe that the output has a 60 Hz ripple,
questions.explanation: Healthy bridge on 60 Hz mains gives 120 Hz ripple. Seeing 60 Hz ripple means it's now operating as half-wave — diagnostic signature of an open diode (see Q36).
